name: Formalism in Art
statement: What makes something art and gives it value is its form, not its subject matter or context.
statementAccent: its form, not its subject matter
meaning: Aesthetic formalism is the view that the aesthetically relevant and artistically significant properties of a work of art are its formal properties, its lines, shapes, colors, and their arrangement or composition, rather than its representational content, subject matter, historical context, the emotions or ideas it expresses, or the intentions behind it. What makes something art, and gives it aesthetic value, is its form, accessible by direct sensation alone, not its content or context. The classic statement is Clive Bell's, in his 1914 book Art, where he argued that the essential quality shared by all visual works of art is significant form, lines and colors combined in a particular way, certain forms and relations of forms, that stir our aesthetic emotions; representation and subject matter, for Bell, are irrelevant to and often a distraction from a work's value as art. Bell's associate Roger Fry, a formalist critic of the Bloomsbury group, championed Post-Impressionism and emphasized form over representation. In music, Eduard Hanslick's On the Musically Beautiful of 1854 defended a musical formalism on which the content of music is tonally moving forms rather than the expression or arousal of emotion. Immanuel Kant, with his emphasis on form and free beauty, is often cited as a precursor, and Clement Greenberg later gave formalism a modernist form. Formalism is criticized for ignoring the representational, expressive, and historical dimensions of art, and Bell's significant form is charged with circularity.
mechanism: Formalism identifies the artistically important features of a work with its form and directs appreciation to those features alone. On this view, what one should attend to in a painting is the organization of its lines, shapes, and colors, the relations and rhythms of its composition, rather than what it depicts, when it was made, or what it means; the form is graspable directly through perception, by sight or hearing, without knowledge of context or subject. Bell made this precise with the notion of significant form, which he defined as the particular combination of lines and colors, the forms and relations of forms, that provokes a special aesthetic emotion, and he took this significant form to be the one quality common to all visual works of art and the sole basis of their value as art, so that a work's representational content is beside the point. Hanslick applied a parallel formalism to music, holding that the beauty and content of a piece consist in its tonally moving forms, the specifically musical relations of tones and their movement, and denying that music's value lies in expressing or arousing emotions. Kant's distinction between free beauty, which requires no concept of what the object should be, and dependent beauty is often read as an ancestor of formalism, privileging design and form over charm and content. Greenberg extended formalism to modernist painting, emphasizing each art's self-critical concentration on the properties of its own medium, such as the flatness of the picture plane. In each case the mechanism is the same: locate the aesthetic in form, and treat content, context, and expression as inessential.

examples.text: Bell held that significant form, lines and colors combined in a particular way, is the one quality common to all visual art.
Hanslick held the content of music is tonally moving forms, not the expression or arousal of emotion.
Greenberg's formalism stressed modernist painting's concentration on its own medium, such as the flatness of the picture plane.

variants.name: Musical formalism

whyItMatters: Formalism is one of the major theories of art and aesthetic value and a powerful counterweight to theories that ground art in representation, expression, or context. By insisting that what matters aesthetically is a work's form, its design, composition, and the relations of its elements, formalism directs attention to the specifically artistic organization of a work rather than to its story, message, or maker, and it thereby offers a clear account of aesthetic value and a discipline of appreciation focused on perceptible structure. Clive Bell's significant form and Eduard Hanslick's musical formalism were highly influential, shaping modern criticism and helping to make sense of art, such as abstract and non-representational work, whose value plainly does not lie in what it depicts. Formalism also fits and helped articulate the modernist emphasis, in Greenberg and others, on each medium's distinctive formal possibilities. At the same time, formalism has been a productive foil, provoking anti-formalist arguments, such as Kendall Walton's demonstration that a work's aesthetic properties depend on the art-historical category under which it is perceived, that context, therefore, is aesthetically relevant. As the view that form is the seat of artistic value, formalism is a central position in aesthetics.

working.text: focus appreciation on a work's lines, shapes, colors, and composition, graspable by direct perception.
treat representation, subject matter, context, and expression as aesthetically inessential.
locate the work's value as art in its formal organization, its significant form or tonally moving forms.

limits: Formalism faces powerful objections centered on everything it sets aside. Critics argue that it wrongly ignores the representational, expressive, historical, and cognitive dimensions of art, which are plainly part of how many works mean and move us, so that confining aesthetic relevance to form leaves out much of what matters in art. Bell's significant form is charged with circularity: he defines significant form as what provokes the aesthetic emotion and the aesthetic emotion as the response to significant form, so neither is independently specified. The strongest general challenge is anti-formalist. Kendall Walton, in his 1970 essay Categories of Art, argued that a work's aesthetic properties depend on the art-historical category under which it is correctly perceived, so that context and history, not form alone, help fix aesthetic character, and Arthur Danto pressed that perceptually indistinguishable objects can differ in art status, which pure formalism cannot explain. Some datings and attributions reward care: Bell's Art is usually dated 1914 though some sources say 1913, Hanslick's treatise dates to 1854, Walton's essay to 1970, and Greenberg is best cited from his own writings rather than a single encyclopedia entry. So formalism robustly locates artistic value in form, understood as an influential view challenged by the aesthetic relevance of content and context and by the circularity of significant form.
misreadings: Formalism is not the claim that artworks have no content or subject matter, only that these are aesthetically inessential compared with form. It is not merely a preference for abstract art, since it makes a general claim about where artistic value lies, applying to representational works too. And Bell's significant form is not an independently defined property, given the circularity objection, so treating formalism as denying that art has content, as only about abstraction, or as resting on a clearly defined significant form, misreads the view.
origin: The view, given its classic statement by Clive Bell's significant form in Art (1914) and by Hanslick's musical formalism, that the artistically significant properties of a work are its formal properties rather than its content or context.
